newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Gulf states seen dragging feet on investment.
newsitem.headline: Gulf states seen dragging feet on investment.

text.p: Gulf Arab states are moving too slowly to lure foreign and local investment and should overhaul regulations to boost investor confidence in their oil-rich economies, officials and financial experts said on Sunday.

"We are moving in the right direction but not as quickly as we should. We need speed. The size of the market is a bit small, not only for foreign investors, but local investors," Bahrain Stock Exchange director Fawzi Behzad told Reuters.
"If you could make all the money invested abroad come back overnight it will not find room for real investment," he added.

The Gulf economies are dominated by the government sector, and although Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates all speak of a bigger private sector role, in many cases the privatisation wheels are turning very slowly.

"We have to believe in foreign investment in the local economy. The time has come for Gulf states to take advantage of the interest that has been created over the years for foreign investors to invest in the local economies," Behzad said.

Behzad and other experts, speaking on the sidelines of a regional banking conference, said Gulf states needed rules on greater financial transparency and to ease restrictions on foreign cash to create an attractive investment climate.

Several experts said the estimated $350 billion in Gulf Arab money invested abroad underscored the predicament of Gulf states which are struggling to push the private sector's role and attract foreigners to diversify their oil-dominated economies.
One Gulf national who has invested abroad said it would take more than just serious privatisation efforts and more attractive laws to boost investor confidence.

"Everyone is an agent and people who are not are losing out. They have entrepreneurial skills that they can't use. Agencies are squeezing the market," he said, referring to family-owned enterprises that serve as agents for everything from luxurious cars to hardware supplies.
Obstacles to greater foreign investment range from a lack of financial disclosure to rules restricting foreign investment in local stock markets and companies, experts said.

"It's not easy to invest in this area. As far as I know, 300 shares are listed in the whole GCC area. Turnover is small... (it) is one fifth of Singapore...which means foreigners are not attracted to investing in these stock markets," Yoh Kurosawa, chairman of The Industrial Bank of Japan Limited said.

One Gulf-based investment consultant said Qatar offers the most promise for foreign investors because of its lucrative gas projects and willingness to allow foreign companies to take a leading role in its energy projects.
"Qatar is the main one in the foreseeable future," he said.
Qatar and foreign companies are pumping more than $10 billion into the country's gas projects to capitalise on soaring Asian power demand over the next 20 years.
